query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Switching the feedstock from a 15–45 μm particle size distribution to a coarser distribution (e.g., 30–75 μm) will overcome the thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and keeping as-sprayed oxidation minimal.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy bond coat deposited using 15–45 μm feedstock by thermal-spray deposition.
generation.intervention: Use a coarser powder feedstock with an increased average particle size (targeting approximately 30–75 μm) while keeping all other processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Deposition by thermal-spray under standard operating conditions for aero-engine bond coats and subsequent high-temperature cycling typical of thermal barrier coating service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Larger particles produce thicker molten splats upon impact due to higher mass and lower surface-to-volume ratio, which helps reduce in-flight oxidation and promotes improved deposition efficiency.
generation.mechanism: Increasing the particle size enhances mass deposition per splat and limits the relative oxidation during flight because of the reduced exposed surface area. This results in a thicker, cohesive bond coat with microstructural integrity similar to that achieved with finer powder, yet with the required overall thickness.
generation.predicted_outcome: A coating with increased overall thickness compared to the baseline (15–45 μm feedstock) while showing minimal additional oxidation and retaining the desired phase structure and adhesion properties.
generation.baseline: The original coating deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock, which falls short of the required thickness.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only when the particle size is increased within an optimal range; excessively large particles could lead to incomplete melting or adverse defects, and too high oxidation would compromise the coating. The process must maintain depositional energy and environmental controls to prevent excess oxidation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the thickness improvement and the detailed interplay with in-flight oxidation are uncertain and may depend on fine-tuning of spray parameters alongside the new feedstock distribution.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct thermal-spray depositions on identical substrates under controlled conditions while varying only the feedstock particle size. Compare coatings made with the baseline 15–45 μm feedstock and with the modified 30–75 μm feedstock. Analyze the coatings using cross-sectional microscopy and X-ray diffraction to evaluate thickness, phase integrity, and oxidation states.
measurements: Oxide content and phase identification via XRD
Microstructural features and splat morphology via optical microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coating produced with the coarser feedstock fails to achieve a statistically significant increase in thickness (e.g., less than a 10% improvement over the baseline) or exhibits increased oxidation levels that compromise mechanical integrity compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. Figure 8 shows the surface morphology of the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating. From Figure 8a, it can be seen that the coating showed a rough morphology, which is usually observed on the surfaces of atmospheric plasma sprayed coatings []. It can be observed that at a higher magnification (Figure 8b), most of the splats were fully molten and well flattened, and the outlines of the flattened splats could be observed obviously. Some spherical and droplet-shaped particles with dimensions of less than 10 μm could also be found on the coating surface, which originated from the sputtering of the flying particles when impacting the already formed coating surface.
